:::: {.vcenter}

"A conference is not a reward for work already finished."

## Three questions a laboratory cannot answer

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Why this is an instrument
:::

::: {.cards .feature}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[]{.dot}

### Is the question still open?

Whether someone across the world solved your problem eight months ago and has not published it yet.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[]{.dot}

### Does the argument survive contact?

Whether your interpretation holds when a stranger who has no reason to be kind attacks it.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[]{.dot}

### Who would work with you?

Which people have the instrument, the sample, or the model you are missing — and would say yes.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
If a meeting cannot answer at least one of these for the work you have right now, it is tourism.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:03–12:06] The argument

Three things the lab cannot give you: what is unpublished right now; an attack from
someone with no reason to be kind; access to capability you do not own.

Land "then it is tourism" lightly. Do not lecture on it.
:::

## Choosing the right meeting {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 1 · 8 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
Match the venue to the stage the work is at, not to the prestige you would like.
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:08] Part 1

"The first mistake happens months before the trip."

The failure mode: three months of data → the biggest meeting in the field → a poster
among nine hundred → four conversations. Do not name anyone.
:::

## Three stages, three kinds of meeting

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 1
:::

::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card .c-sky}
[Early]{.eyebrow}

### An idea and a trend

Domestic or regional meeting, small session. The goal is criticism, not visibility — you want the awkward question now, while the design can still change.

**Take the poster.** Thirty minutes per person beats three.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[Middle]{.eyebrow}

### A result you believe

Specialist international meeting in your subfield. The goal is to test the interpretation against people who know the system as well as you do.

**Fight for the oral slot.** This is where collaborations start.
:::

::: {.card .c-teal}
[Late]{.eyebrow}

### A paper near submission

Large flagship meeting, or an invited talk. The goal is priority, visibility, and reviewer familiarity.

**Least useful for improving the work.** It is already fixed.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
One question decides it: what would have to happen at this meeting for the trip to have been worth it?
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:08–12:13] Stage → venue

Early: small meeting, and take the poster — thirty minutes per person, not three.
Middle: specialist meeting, fight for the oral slot. Spend most of the time here.
Late: visibility only. The argument is already fixed.

DO — put the closing question on the board.
:::

## Reading a meeting before you commit

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 1
:::

::: {.numbered .n4}
1. **Who chairs the sessions?** Look at the symposium organizers, not the plenary list. Organizers decide who is in the room.
2. **Where does the abstract end up?** Reviewed abstract, full proceedings paper, or nothing? This decides whether the work is still publishable later.
3. **Who came last time?** Find last year's programme. If the three groups you cite most are absent, it is the wrong meeting.
4. **What is the cost per useful contact?** Registration plus travel, divided by the number of people you realistically expect to talk to.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.flag}
Warning signs — an invitation email that flatters you · a scope covering five unrelated fields · a fee due before review · a venue that changes city every year · no named programme committee
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:13–12:16] Due diligence

Dwell on check 2: full proceedings can block the journal submission later.
Check 3 is the cheapest — open last year's programme, search the groups you cite.

DO — say these invitations arrive weekly. Forward the doubtful ones to me.
:::

## The months before you travel {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 2 · 8 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
Everything that decides the value of the trip is decided before you board.
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:16] Part 2

"From here the clock runs backward from the abstract deadline, not forward from today."
:::

## Plan backward from the abstract deadline

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 2
:::

::: {.steps}
::: {.step .c-teal}
[T−6 months]{.n}
[Decide the claim]{.h}
[Name the one sentence you intend to defend. Identify the experiment still missing to support it.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-sky}
[T−4 months]{.n}
[Close the data gap]{.h}
[Run the missing measurement. Assume one repeat will fail, and budget for it.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-amber}
[T−3 months]{.n}
[Submit the abstract]{.h}
[Promise the result you will have. Not the topic you are working on.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-sage}
[T−6 weeks]{.n}
[Build the materials]{.h}
[Figures at final quality. Draft slides or poster. Travel booked, paperwork started.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-rust}
[T−2 weeks]{.n}
[Rehearse and target]{.h}
[Two full rehearsals with questions. Write down the people and sessions you are going for.]{.d}
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
The abstract is a contract, not a title. "The effect of X on Y was investigated" tells the committee you do not yet know what you found.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:16–12:21] Backward planning

Tell them to copy this timeline.

T−3 is where it breaks: people submit a topic because the data are not in. The fix is
at T−6 — decide the claim while there is still time to earn it.

DO — read both abstracts aloud. "The effect of additive on zinc anodes was
investigated" versus "2 wt% suppresses dendrite nucleation and triples cycle life".
:::

## Four things to have ready before you fly

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 2
:::

::: {.cards .stack .numbered-stack}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[1]{.numdot}

### A 30-second introduction

Who you are, which group, what problem you work on. Rehearsed until it bores you. You will use it forty times.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[2]{.numdot}

### A 2-minute version of the work

Question, approach, key result, why it matters. No slides. This is what you say standing next to a coffee urn.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[3]{.numdot}

### A one-page summary to leave behind

Title, one figure, three results, your email, a QR code to the preprint. People lose business cards; they keep paper with a figure on it.
:::

::: {.card .c-sage}
[4]{.numdot}

### A named target list

Five people you want to meet. Three sessions you will not miss. One question you want answered. Written down, on your phone.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:21–12:24] What to carry

Bad: "master student, I work on batteries."
Good: "I work on why zinc anodes fail in the first fifty cycles, not the last."

Item 4 separates an active trip from a passive one. Email two of the five people
before you travel — almost nobody does, so the hit rate is high.
:::

## Designing for the time you are given {.dark .divider .c-amber background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 3 · 10 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
A twelve-minute talk is not a short seminar. A poster is not a paper on a wall.
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:24] Part 3

"Talks fail by being too full. Posters fail by being unreadable from two metres."
:::

## Anatomy of a 12 + 3 talk

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 3
:::

::: {.dots}
- **2 min · Why should anyone care?** The problem, in the audience's language. One sentence they could repeat at dinner.
- **3 min · What exactly did you do?** Enough method for a stranger to believe the data. Not the full protocol.
- **5 min · What did you find?** The core. Two or three figures, each with one message said out loud.
- **2 min · What does it mean?** Interpretation, the honest limitation, and the one thing you would do next.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
One message per slide, written as the slide title · about one slide per minute · memorize only the first 60 seconds and the last 30 · finish 30 seconds early
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:24–12:29] Talk structure

Results get 5 of the 12 minutes, method gets 3. Most student talks invert this.

Memorize only the first 60 seconds and the last 30 — that is where attention peaks.
Finish 30 seconds early; session chairs remember who gave time back.
:::

## A poster is read at three distances

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 3
:::

::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[3 m]{.big}

### The title does the work

Three seconds, while walking past. Write the finding, not the topic. *"Additive X triples zinc anode life"* stops people. *"A study of additives for zinc anodes"* does not.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[1 m]{.big}

### One figure carries the claim

A visitor who stops gives you thirty seconds of silent reading. One large central figure, labelled so it works without you standing beside it.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[arm's length]{.big}

### The detail is there if asked

Method, conditions and controls in small type at the edges. Present for the specialist, invisible to everyone else.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.flag}
Stand beside your poster, not in front of it · open with "May I give you the two-minute version?" · put your name and email large enough to photograph
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:29–12:34] Poster

The title is the only part most people ever read. Make it a finding, not a topic.
Stand beside the poster, not in front of it. Offer the two-minute version.

DO — if time allows, take one real title from the room and rewrite it live. Two at
most, then move on.
:::

## Handling questions in English {.dark .divider .c-amber background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 4 · 9 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
Nobody in that room is grading your grammar. They are watching how you think.
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:34] Part 4

"Nobody is grading your grammar. They are watching how you think."

Fluency is not the requirement. Being understood is — and that is structure and
speed, not vocabulary.
:::

## Almost every question is one of five

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 4
:::

::: {.cards .g3 .wrap}
::: {.card .c-sky}
[1]{.numdot}

### Clarification

*"What was the scan rate?"* Easy. Answer in one sentence and stop talking.
:::

::: {.card .c-sage}
[2]{.numdot}

### Challenge to the method

*"How do you know it is not an artefact?"* Name the control you ran — or concede that you have not run it.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[3]{.numdot}

### Alternative explanation

*"Could this be X instead?"* Often the most useful question you will get. Say what evidence would separate the two.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[4]{.numdot}

### Scope and generality

*"Does this work for other systems?"* Answer where the boundary is, not a hopeful yes.
:::

::: {.card .c-teal}
[5]{.numdot}

### "Have you seen my paper?"

Rarely hostile. Thank them, write the reference down where they can see you do it, and mean it.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:34–12:38] Five types

Type 3 is a free reviewer comment months before submission. Do not defend — say what
measurement would separate the two explanations.

Type 5 usually wants a citation. Write it down where they can see you do it.
:::

## One structure for every answer

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 4
:::

::: {.steps}
::: {.step .c-teal}
[1]{.n}
[Acknowledge]{.h}
["Thank you, that is an important point." Buys three seconds and costs nothing.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-amber}
[2]{.n}
[Restate]{.h}
["So you are asking whether the capacity loss comes from the anode rather than the electrolyte?" Lets them correct you cheaply.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-rust}
[3]{.n}
[Answer in one sentence]{.h}
[The direct answer first. Not the background, not the history.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-sage}
[4]{.n}
[Offer the detail]{.h}
["I can show the control experiment if that is useful." Let them choose to go deeper.]{.d}
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
*"Could you repeat the question, please?"* · *"I want to make sure I understood — do you mean …?"* · *"I do not know. What would settle it is …"* · *"That is a fair criticism, and here is what we did about it."* · *"Could we continue this at the coffee break?"*
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:38–12:43] Answer structure

Step 2 is the one that saves you: restating buys thinking time and reads as courtesy.

"I do not know. What would settle it is …" costs nothing. Pretending costs the room.

Slow down — under stress non-native speakers speed up, which is backwards.

DO — demonstrate on a volunteer's hostile question, all four steps.
:::

## The first 48 hours after you return {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 5 · 6 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
This is where most conference value is lost — quietly, and permanently.
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:43] Part 5

"You will be tired, and there will be four hundred emails."

Do nothing in the first two days and the trip converts itself into a certificate.
:::

## Convert the trip before it evaporates

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 5
:::

::: {.cards .stack}
::: {.card .c-sky}
[]{.dot}

### Before you land

Write the trip note. Two pages on the plane, while it is fresh: what you learned, who you met, what changed in your plan.
:::

::: {.card .c-sage}
[]{.dot}

### Within 24 hours

Send the follow-ups. Three sentences each: where we met, what we discussed, what I propose next. Attach the one-pager. After a week they no longer remember your face.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[]{.dot}

### Within 48 hours

Turn questions into work. Every question you could not answer becomes an experiment, a control, a paper to read, or a paragraph to rewrite.
:::

::: {.card .c-teal}
[]{.dot}

### Within a week

Report back to the group. Fifteen minutes at group meeting is how one funded trip becomes useful to twelve people.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
Send the follow-up emails from the airport. Waiting until you feel rested means waiting until it is too late.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:43–12:47] Closing the loop

The trip note is the only durable record that will exist.
The follow-up is three sentences, within a day — your face has a shelf life.

Reporting back at group meeting is also how you justify the next trip.
:::

## Judge the trip by what changed {.dark background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
If you remember three things
:::

::: {.numbered .n3}
1. **Choose on purpose** The meeting must match the stage the work is at. Prestige is not a criterion.
2. **Design for the time you are given** Twelve minutes, one message per slide. Three metres, a title that states a finding.
3. **Close the loop within 48 hours** Trip note, follow-up emails, questions turned into experiments.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.statement-sub}
A conference is a research instrument. Before the next one you attend, write down what you intend it to measure.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
[12:47–13:00] Close and questions

Three points, then stop. Do not summarize the summary.

If the room is silent: "who has a conference in the next six months, and what are you
worried about?"

DO — offer to read a draft abstract sent at least three weeks ahead. Say "three
weeks", or you will get them the night before.
:::
